body: Yes, that sounds very likely. Syncthing itself has no issue with files with non-ASCII characters in them; everything on the wire is UTF-8, and it assumes that filesystems on Linux are as well (with special handling for Mac which uses the "wrong" kind of unicode normalization). Is this a standard ext4 filesystem, no funny mount options related to character set (if any such exist) or anything like that? What's the node on the other side?

This is a standard ext4 filesystem, no interesting mount options:

```
/dev/sda6 on /mnt/Storage type ext4 (rw,nosuid,nodev,relatime,data=ordered)
```

which are standard on linux. The node on the other side is the exact same, ext4 linux.

EDIT: Also, I'd just like to note again that the issue doesn't present itself when there are no nodes to sync with. It only occurs when I allow Syncthing to sync with the other nodes.

I can't reproduce this... For me it works fine to sync a file called åäöèúï.txt between Mac and two Ubuntus. Can you do an `ls | od -at x1` on all nodes where that file / those files are present, so we can see how that filename is actually encoded (and I can try to reproduce with that)?

On the Corei7 computer:

ls Capítulo\ 1\ Yo\ Soy\ Betty\ La\ Fea\ Completo.mp4 | od -at x1

```

0000040  sp   C   o   m   p   l   e   t   o   .   m   p   4  nl

```

On the thinkpad:

```
0000000   C   a   p   i   L soh   t   u   l   o  sp   1  sp   Y   o  sp
         43  61  70  69  cc  81  74  75  6c  6f  20  31  20  59  6f  20
0000020   S   o   y  sp   B   e   t   t   y  sp   L   a  sp   F   e   a
         53  6f  79  20  42  65  74  74  79  20  4c  61  20  46  65  61
0000040  sp   C   o   m   p   l   e   t   o   .   m   p   4  nl
         20  43  6f  6d  70  6c  65  74  6f  2e  6d  70  34  0a
0000056
```

Let me know if you want to see the other files done too.

@calmh Also, as promised earlier today, here are the logs using strace for about 5-10 minutes on the two machines in question. They are long and boring, so I hope you enjoy them :-).

https://mega.co.nz/#!xFljVZQa!TGyrAOWHBqvXNf8ihfiHGK4exPs9Y1OjA3v-Mzk895Q

Right, so the í in there is `69 cc 81` which is UTF-8 normalization form D, unexpected on Linux and standard on Mac. We would expect to see `c3 ad` instead. Anyway, that's probably the problem, and of course syncthing should handle it. I'll see what I can do to reproduce and fix. Oh and thanks for the logs, hopefully they won't be necessary ;)

(Oh and before anyone says "why don't you just ignore the encoding and just copy the name", I want an ä from Linux to actually show up as an ä on my Mac, and that requires handling encodings correctly. The encoding also occasionally gets "fixed" by the filesystem so we write one filename and read another back, which doesn't end well. In fact, it's probably something like that that happens here, but internal to syncthing.)

So, I reproduced this easy enough now that we know what the problem is. Syncthing normalizes file names to UTF-8 NFC over the wire. The Linux binary expects local filenames to be in UTF-8 NFC and doesn't convert what it reads from disk. So the source node gets a request for the filename in NFC, but the filename on disk (and local index) is actually encoded in NFD, so the request for file data fails and the sync fails.

I'm not sure what the correct fix is.

We could re-encode file names to the correct/expected encoding for the platform, like we do on Windows and Mac. _But_ on Linux it's actually valid (if stupid) to have two files both called `Hí` but with different encoding of the í - they'll _look_ the same and you won't be able to type the name of one of them, but they can live on disk. That's not possible on Mac and Windows, so we run into the same issue as if you had two filenames that differ only in case (also unsolved).

rename.to: Issues syncing files with names in unexpected charset encodings

body:
@calmh Even though its valid, if it isn't the way that it is normally done, perhaps it is better to re-encode the names. Windows and Mac don't even have the option, and even if Linux gives the option, if it is something rare, then why not go with the normal case?

If nothing else, it would be good if at least syncthing could inform me about why it has a problem with the file (so that I can rename it or something).

Oh yeah, it should be handled _somehow_, no doubt about that. Problem is, normalizing the name is not enough; it would essentially need to rename the file to the "correct" encoding. Otherwise we would need to remember both the normalized name and whatever we found on disk and keep the mapping between them. I don't like silently changing stuff on the source, so perhaps in this case we should simply check the encoding and emit a warning "unexpected filename encoding; check and consider renaming" and simply ignore the file. Then again, that's not great either because if the same file exists on another node (with correct encoding) we'll pick that up and sync it, effectively creating a copy of the file with the same name in another encoding...

It seems almost as if the best solution is if Syncthing can notify the user of this issue, and offer to rename it. Otherwise, it would simply have to ignore it. If files exist on other nodes, they will want to sync with the Linux computer. Unless the Linux computer refuses to sync the file, itll take the file with the standard encoding set anyway. Even ignoring it won't really work. I suspect the user will have to take action in this case.

In fact, this is basically how I have worked around this problem, was just to simply change the character to one where Syncthing does sync the file properly. I suspect users will simply do this if they are notified to, if they are paying attention.

IMHO, a simple solution would be to detect issues with strange normalizations, show a warning, and then also refuse to accept files with alternate encodings.  If this would prevent a repository from reaching 100% sync, it would also be a good way of exposing the problem to other nodes in the system.
